title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: PLAC — Adam's first; animal analogy
pass_a_gloss: PLAC. He did not express the conclusion: for from those two premises that which it fell to him to prove cannot be concluded. For it is not a matter of every violation of the law, but of such a one, namely that first of Adam, nor of any privation of justice you please, but of the privation of the justice with which Adam was endowed before the fall. For of this violation and privation the minor proposition of my argument is to be understood. Therefore either the Learned Man's Minor ought to have been universal, or to be understood namely of that privation and violation. Since neither has been done, nothing opposing me can be concluded. Next by a like argument countless most true propositions could be refuted, even this, man is an animal. For those things are not one and the same which in the thing itself can be separated. But something can be an animal and yet not be a man.
pass_b_english: Placeus. He never states the conclusion; those two premises cannot yield what he needs to prove. The question is not every law-breaking, but Adam's first; not any loss of righteousness, but the loss of the righteousness Adam had before the fall. My minor is about that breach and that loss. Garissoles' minor must either be universal or name that case; neither done, nothing against me follows.
The same pattern would overturn endless true propositions—even "man is an animal." Things that can really be separated are not identical; something can be an animal and yet not a man.
source_text: PLAC. Conclusionem non expressit: haud enim ex duabus illis praemissis concludi potest id quod ei probandum incumbebat. Agitur enim non de omni violatione legis, sed de tali, nempe prima illa Adami, nec de qualibet privatione justitiae, sed de privatione justitiae qua praeditus erat ante lapsum Adamus. De hac enim violatione & privatione intelligenda est argumenti mei propositio minor. Aut igitur universalem esse oportebat Viri Docti Minorem, aut nominatim de illa privatione & violatione intelligi. Neutrum cum sit factum, nihil potest concludi mihi repugnans. Deinde simili argumento possent infinitae propositiones verissimae refelli, etiam ista, homo est animal. Nam ea non sunt unum & idem quae reapse possunt separari. Atqui potest aliquid esse animal, nec tamen esse homo.
